paragraphs: Supervised contrastive learning builds representations using groups of labeled examples. In practice, these groups repeatedly draw from the same finite dataset, so they are statistically dependent. This paper studies how much data learning requires when that dependence is accounted for, especially when there are many classes with highly unequal frequencies.

Earlier analysis required the risk estimate for every class to concentrate uniformly. That made its error bounds sensitive to the rarest class, even when rare classes contribute little to average population risk. The authors first establish a sample-complexity bound that scales with the number of classes, regardless of how probability is distributed among them.

They then introduce another risk estimator that captures concentration across classes rather than imposing the same requirement on each class separately. This yields sharper guarantees for extreme multiclass problems, particularly long-tailed distributions. Under stated mild assumptions on class distributions, sample complexity becomes O(k), where k is the number of examples per contrastive tuple. The advance is a more favorable theoretical account of learning from dependent tuples.
icml-2026-a-refined-generalization-analy.tldr: New risk estimators give sharper sample-complexity guarantees for supervised contrastive learning with many unevenly represented classes.

paragraphs: Strategic classification studies prediction when the people being evaluated can respond to the decision rule. A common starting assumption is that everyone knows the classifier. This paper instead considers a regulatory setting that requires some disclosure while allowing the system to keep part of its decision process private.

The authors formalize partial disclosure through ambiguity, a concept drawn from robust mechanism design. The system announces a set or range of possible classifiers but privately chooses which one to use. Learning therefore involves two connected decisions: choosing the classifier and choosing the uncertainty that surrounds it. That uncertainty becomes part of the strategic environment to which evaluated individuals respond.

The paper examines how this additional choice changes learning and develops efficient algorithms for computing best responses and training classifiers. It also empirically explores strategic behavior and resulting outcomes in this setting. Its contribution is a framework for analyzing partial disclosure as an explicit design decision, rather than assuming that full disclosure is already settled. The abstract does not claim that ambiguity always improves outcomes.
icml-2026-ambiguous-strategic-classifica.tldr: The paper models partial classifier disclosure as a learnable choice and develops algorithms for strategic classification under that ambiguity.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based anomaly detectors can be computationally complicated because they work through multiple noise levels and denoising steps. This paper asks whether tabular anomaly detection needs that generative machinery. It develops a simpler method that learns to denoise at a fixed noise level, without targeting the generation of new data.

The method trains a self-supervised denoising predictor and uses preconditioning with an explicit linear reference channel. Its anomaly score comes from expected deviations under repeated perturbations. The resulting signal serves as a proxy for stability, rather than simply measuring how poorly an input can be reconstructed or how far it lies from a learned data manifold.

On ADBench, the authors report state-of-the-art results, with improvements of 1.22% in AUCROC and 1.13% in AUCPR over existing baselines. These findings support the usefulness of a single-step denoising objective for this benchmark. The computational simplification concerns the denoising formulation: scoring still involves repeated perturbations. The broader contribution is showing that effective anomaly detection can draw on denoising without requiring a full generative diffusion schedule.
icml-2026-denoising-without-diffusion-fi.tldr: A fixed-noise denoiser detects tabular anomalies through perturbation stability and outperforms existing baselines on ADBench.

paragraphs: Flow and diffusion models can generate high-quality samples, yet adapting their outputs to a reward after training can be costly and brittle. This paper treats adaptability as a property to build into the generative model. Diamond Maps are designed to support efficient reward alignment when samples are generated.

The central design combines two features: compressing many simulation steps into a single-step sampler and retaining stochasticity. The first reduces the work needed to generate samples; the second preserves randomness that the authors identify as necessary for optimal reward adaptation. This combination distinguishes the proposed approach from acceleration that does not preserve the required stochastic behavior.

Diamond Maps also support efficient, consistent value-function estimation, making search, Sequential Monte Carlo, and guidance more scalable. The experiments show that the models can be learned efficiently by distilling GLASS Flows, with stronger reward alignment and better scaling than existing alignment methods. These results support a route toward rapid adaptation to varied preferences and constraints at inference time, while the empirical comparisons establish the reported gains in the tested settings.
icml-2026-diamond-maps-efficient-reward-.tldr: Diamond Maps combine fast sampling with preserved stochasticity to make inference-time reward alignment more efficient.

paragraphs: Conformal methods can filter language-model claims using thresholds calibrated on held-out data, providing statistical control over hallucination rates. For multistep reasoning, however, individual claims also depend on earlier claims. Coherent Factuality addresses this by representing an answer as a dependency graph and checking claims together with their logical ancestors.

The difficulty is that the original procedure is not differentiable, which prevents directly learning better scorers through that procedure. Its hand-crafted scorers can remove nearly 60% of true claims at high reliability levels. This paper introduces Differentiable Coherent Factuality, a differentiable relaxation that makes scorer learning possible while provably recovering the original algorithm’s guarantees.

On two reasoning datasets, the authors report up to 141% improvement in claim retention while maintaining reliability guarantees. The practical benefit is keeping more of an answer’s useful content under the same kind of reliability requirement. The contribution connects training with structured factuality checking: it improves the scoring component while preserving attention to dependencies between claims, rather than treating every statement as an isolated decision.
icml-2026-differentiable-conformal-train.tldr: A differentiable factuality filter learns to retain more reasoning claims while preserving conformal reliability guarantees.

paragraphs: Offline imitation learning uses recorded behavior to learn a policy. This paper considers datasets containing three kinds of demonstrations: expert behavior, explicitly undesirable behavior, and behavior without either label. Its starting point is that examples of what to avoid carry useful information that conventional expert-and-unlabeled formulations can overlook.

DualCOIL expresses the learning objective through a difference of KL divergences between state-action visitation distributions. These distributions describe which situations and actions occur under different behaviors. The formulation brings positive and negative demonstrations into one objective, allowing the policy-learning problem to account for both desirable and undesirable patterns without adversarial training.

A difference-of-convex objective is not generally convex, but the authors prove convexity when expert demonstrations outweigh undesirable demonstrations. That condition enables the practical, stable training objective described in the paper. Experiments on standard offline imitation-learning benchmarks show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution combines a way to use explicitly negative demonstrations with a conditional mathematical result that makes the resulting optimization more tractable.
icml-2026-dualcoil-offline-imitation-lea.tldr: DualCOIL learns from expert and undesirable demonstrations using a non-adversarial objective that becomes convex when expert demonstrations outweigh undesirable ones.

paragraphs: Distributed training can spend substantial time waiting for workers to exchange updates, especially over limited-bandwidth connections. DiLoCo reduces how often workers communicate, but its outer synchronization still transfers considerable data and is vulnerable to slow workers and temporary failures. This paper changes how that synchronization is performed.

The authors replace exact agreement with approximate synchronization through mixing, also called gossip. They split synchronization into two parts. A non-blocking mixing step overlaps communication with computation without introducing staleness, while a blocking step brings workers into closer agreement. The balance between these steps provides a control over compute utilization and optimization stability.

Experiments on language models with up to a billion parameters in low-bandwidth settings show substantially better compute utilization than DiLoCo. Training progress ranges from comparable to closely matching DiLoCo, and the method is more robust to failures. The result matters because communication efficiency is evaluated alongside learning progress: keeping workers busy is useful only if their updates remain sufficiently coordinated. Approximate agreement provides a tunable way to manage that balance.
icml-2026-factored-gossip-diloco-reducin.tldr: Splitting DiLoCo synchronization into overlapping and blocking gossip steps improves utilization and failure robustness in low-bandwidth training.

paragraphs: An assistant can correct a bad action without correcting the misunderstanding that caused it. This paper targets that underlying source of repeated mistakes. SENSEI infers misconceptions from a person’s interaction behavior and uses those inferences to provide targeted suggestions intended to be minimal while still sufficient to correct the problem.

The framework operates over a structured representation of knowledge. This gives it a way to locate gaps in understanding rather than intervening only on individual actions or complete trajectories. The distinction matters for tasks that unfold over many steps: a misunderstanding can influence several decisions, so guidance aimed at its source can address a recurring pattern.

Across three long-horizon tasks, SENSEI separates multiple overlapping misconceptions despite being trained only on cases containing a single misconception. This demonstrates zero-shot compositional generalization in those evaluations. A user study also finds that it identifies real human misconceptions and improves task performance, successfully correcting 90% of student misconceptions. Together, these findings support knowledge-level diagnosis as a practical basis for interpretable assistance.
icml-2026-fix-the-mind-not-the-move-inte.tldr: SENSEI diagnoses misconceptions from behavior and gives targeted guidance, correcting 90% of student misconceptions in a user study.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can generate several tokens in parallel and use context from both directions. But independently sampling those tokens can miss dependencies between them, breaking syntax or structures that span multiple tokens. This is especially relevant to code generation, where nearby choices often need to fit together precisely.

CoDiLA combines diffusion with a small auxiliary autoregressive model. The diffusion model supplies latent representations, and the auxiliary model handles local decoding sequentially within a block. Generation can still proceed in parallel across blocks, while the local decoder models relationships among tokens inside each block. The design also retains bidirectional modeling across blocks.

The authors report that a compact auxiliary model, including a 0.6-billion-parameter example, effectively eliminates coherence artifacts in their evaluations. On code-generation benchmarks, the method establishes a new accuracy–speed Pareto frontier, improving the available tradeoffs between those objectives. The main insight is that parallel generation can coexist with local sequential structure: a comparatively small decoder can handle dependencies that independent token sampling fails to capture.
icml-2026-locally-coherent-parallel-deco.tldr: CoDiLA adds a small local autoregressive decoder to diffusion language models, improving code coherence while retaining parallel generation.

paragraphs: As a Transformer processes longer contexts, individual attention probabilities can become small. That raises a question: are tokens becoming indistinguishable, or are their relative differences still informative? This paper formalizes token distinguishability in terms of context length and embedding dimension, using Aitchison distance to measure relationships among attention probabilities.

Under Gaussian queries and keys, the authors show that distinguishability approaches a finite, nonzero limit even for long contexts. Small absolute attention values therefore need not imply disappearing relative distinctions under this model. They also use the linear relationship between inverse-temperature scaling and Aitchison distance to analyze how strongly logits must be scaled to sharpen attention.

The resulting lower bound is Omega(sqrt(log L)), where L denotes context length. This is a necessary scaling bound in the analysis, rather than a claim that this scaling alone always suffices. The paper also demonstrates Aitchison distance as a practical alternative to entropy for monitoring training and inference. Its value is capturing the full relative structure of attention, including small probability components.
icml-2026-modelling-attention-with-aitch.tldr: Aitchison geometry shows that relative token distinctions can persist in long-context attention and yields a lower bound on sharpening logits.

paragraphs: Discovering causal relationships from observations often requires strong assumptions about how data were generated. One common assumption is that disturbances are non-Gaussian. This paper examines another source of information: multiple related views of the same system, whose relationships can help distinguish causal structures that a single view leaves unresolved.

The authors introduce a multiview linear structural equation model that can use correlations across views in place of non-Gaussian disturbances. They prove identifiability for acyclic models, meaning that the causal model can be determined under the proposed assumptions. The result therefore depends on the multiview structure and the acyclic linear setting; it does not eliminate the need for assumptions.

They then develop algorithms inspired by DirectLiNGAM, PairwiseLiNGAM, and ICA-LiNGAM, adapting single-view approaches to this source of information. Validation includes simulations and neuroimaging applications, where the methods estimate causal graphs among brain regions. The contribution is a theoretical and algorithmic route to causal discovery that uses relationships between views to relax a familiar distributional requirement.
icml-2026-multi-view-causal-discovery-wi.tldr: Correlations across related views enable identifiable causal discovery in an acyclic linear model without requiring non-Gaussian disturbances.

paragraphs: Evaluating a new model on every benchmark query can be expensive because both generating responses and assessing them require resources. This paper uses information that evaluation pipelines may already possess: cached responses from previously tested models. The goal is to predict a new model’s benchmark performance using fewer fresh queries.

The approach relies on Data Kernel Perspective Space, or DKPS, which measures relationships between models in a black-box setting. Those relationships let the evaluation method use reference-model responses when estimating performance. The authors prove query efficiency under certain conditions, providing theoretical support for when cached information can reduce the amount of new evaluation needed.

Empirically, DKPS-based methods match baseline mean absolute error with substantially smaller query budgets. The paper also introduces an offline query-selection method that chooses queries to maximize goodness-of-fit on reference models. This improves prediction accuracy over random selection. Together, the findings show how previous evaluation work can support both performance estimation and the choice of which questions to ask a new model.
icml-2026-query-efficient-model-evaluati.tldr: Cached responses from earlier models help predict a new model’s benchmark performance accurately with substantially fewer queries.

paragraphs: Hierarchical reinforcement learning aims to organize decisions over longer timescales, but existing methods have struggled to benefit fully from large-scale training. This paper focuses on the practical challenges of running online hierarchical learning in environments that can generate experience quickly. Its proposed algorithm is Scalable Option Learning, or SOL.

SOL is a hierarchical policy-gradient method designed for high throughput. The authors report processing experience 35 times faster than existing hierarchical methods. This matters because a promising decision-making structure must also train efficiently enough to use large experience budgets; otherwise, its computational overhead can restrict the scale at which it is tested.

The researchers train hierarchical agents on 30 billion frames of NetHack experience. Those agents substantially outperform flat agents and show positive scaling trends in the reported experiments. Evaluations on MiniHack and Mujoco provide evidence that SOL applies beyond the main game setting. The combined contribution is an algorithm that makes large-scale hierarchical training practical and empirical evidence that hierarchy can benefit from that scale.
icml-2026-scalable-option-learning-in-hi.tldr: SOL scales hierarchical reinforcement learning to 30 billion NetHack frames with 35-fold higher throughput than existing hierarchical methods.

paragraphs: Error-correcting codes help recover messages corrupted during transmission. SB-ECC treats this recovery as continuous-time denoising: a neural model defines a probability-flow ordinary differential equation that moves a noisy channel observation toward a valid codeword. Parity constraints guide the process toward outputs consistent with the code.

The decoder learns directly from raw signed channel observations across multiple noise levels. It does not require time or signal-to-noise-ratio conditioning, allowing inference without estimating the signal-to-noise ratio first. The numerical solver’s budget provides a direct way to trade decoding latency against accuracy, connecting computational effort to the recovery process.

Across 42 code and signal-to-noise settings, SB-ECC obtains the best bit-error rate in 39. Against the strongest competing baseline, the reported signal-to-noise gain averages 0.17 dB and reaches 0.46 dB. Replacing the Euler solver with DPM preserves the reported negative-log bit-error-rate measure while reducing end-to-end decoding time by 8.86% on average, with a maximum reduction of 12.82%. These findings highlight both decoder quality and the practical importance of solver choice.
icml-2026-score-based-error-correcting-c.tldr: SB-ECC decodes noisy codewords through a learned denoising ODE, achieving the best bit-error rate in 39 of 42 tested settings.

paragraphs: A prompt-injection defense can appear successful by discarding suspicious text, even when the task requires preserving that text through translation or editing. Standard attack-success metrics cannot distinguish this omission from correctly processing the text as data. The paper introduces SecFid to measure security alongside fidelity to the requested transformation.

SecFid makes three behaviors produce distinguishable outputs: following an injected instruction, processing it as content, and ignoring it. Across 1,168 examples and 48 configurations, no tested model or defense achieves both objectives fully. The highest-fidelity model reaches 96.5% fidelity with 47.8% security; the most secure defenses reach 99.3% security with only 71.0%–73.9% fidelity.

Defenses with the same security score can also behave differently: some turn hijacked outputs into faithful processing, while others suppress benign content. A decision-theoretic analysis explains why the appropriate tradeoff depends on deployment-specific costs of hijacking versus dropping text. The findings make fidelity an essential companion to security reporting, because a strong security number alone can conceal substantial damage to the intended task.
icml-2026-securityfidelity-tradeoffs-the.tldr: SecFid shows that prompt-injection defenses can gain security by dropping required content, exposing a deployment-dependent tradeoff with fidelity.

paragraphs: Audio deepfake detectors can struggle with attacks they have not seen during training. The paper attributes part of this problem to spectral bias: networks emphasize low-frequency structure and underuse subtle high-frequency artifacts from generative models. SONAR explicitly connects these two sources of information during representation learning.

The architecture has two paths. An XLSR encoder captures low-frequency content, while learnable, value-constrained high-pass filters extract high-frequency residuals. Frequency cross-attention combines the resulting representations. A Jensen–Shannon alignment loss encourages agreement between low- and high-frequency representations for genuine audio and accentuates inconsistency for generated audio, making their relationship central to detection.

On ASVspoof 2021 and in-the-wild benchmarks, SONAR achieves state-of-the-art performance in the reported single-run setting and converges faster than strong baselines. The significance is that high-frequency information is integrated through a structured learning objective rather than merely added as another feature stream. The results support frequency-guided alignment as a data-driven approach to improving generalization, with the reported evidence grounded in those benchmark evaluations.
icml-2026-sonar-spectral-contrastive-aud.tldr: SONAR improves audio deepfake detection by learning how speech content and high-frequency residuals agree in genuine recordings and diverge in fakes.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts models activate only some experts for each inference, but realizing the performance benefit requires managing which experts are cached in fast memory. This paper introduces SpecMD, a standardized framework for comparing caching strategies across hardware configurations under controlled, realistic constraints. It reproduces and extends previous approaches.

The benchmarking finds that expert access does not fit the locality assumptions behind policies such as least-recently-used and least-frequently-used caching. The authors instead exploit predictable expert-access patterns with a new eviction policy called Least-Stale. Its goal is to avoid collision misses that arise when useful experts are displaced from the cache.

Least-Stale reduces collision misses by up to 85 times relative to LRU. On OLMoE, the paper reports cache hit rates above 88% and up to a 34.7% reduction in time to first token with only 5%, or 0.6 GB, of VRAM cache capacity. These results show why matching cache policy to model access patterns can matter alongside hardware capacity, and SpecMD supplies a framework for examining those interactions.
icml-2026-specmd-a-comprehensive-study-o.tldr: SpecMD benchmarks MoE caching and introduces Least-Stale, which substantially reduces cache misses and first-token latency in reported tests.

paragraphs: Language models can be directed through written prompts or through changes to their internal activations. Activation steering often performs worse than prompting. This paper investigates whether it can improve by learning to reproduce the internal interventions that a steering prompt itself induces, using prompting as the behavior to imitate.

The proposed Prompt Steering Replacement models estimate position-specific steering coefficients. That lets the intervention vary across positions instead of applying the constant coefficients common in existing approaches. Training distills prompt-induced behavior into interpretable activation interventions, connecting a successful external instruction to a structured internal control mechanism.

Experiments cover persona steering and instruction following across multiple language models. PSR consistently outperforms the constant-coefficient interventions tested and reaches performance close to, or above, prompt steering while maintaining interpretability. These results support the usefulness of adapting steering strength by position and learning from the model’s own response to prompts. The demonstrated advantage concerns the evaluated tasks and models, while the broader contribution is a family of interventions trained to mimic prompt-based control.
icml-2026-steer-like-the-llm-activation-.tldr: Prompt Steering Replacement learns position-specific activation interventions that match or approach prompting performance in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can produce a convincing causal explanation without demonstrating the causal structure behind it. This paper separates those abilities using two probes. One measures the linguistic quality of an explanation, while the other requires the model to produce an explicit causal chain before its explanation is assessed.

The Abstraction Gap measures the normalized performance difference between these probes. The authors evaluate eight models on CAGE, which contains 49,500 questions over 5,500 images spanning Pearl’s causal hierarchy. Seven models have gaps above 0.50: their text scores fall between 6 and 8, while their chain scores remain below 2.5.

Fine-tuning on 45,000 chain-annotated examples fails to close the observed gap. However, one evaluated model achieves a near-zero gap, showing that the disparity is not shared by every tested model. The authors connect this variation to pretraining and architectural choices. CAGE’s practical contribution is a diagnostic that makes fluent explanation and explicit causal reasoning separately visible, helping expose weaknesses that ordinary language-quality evaluation can obscure.
icml-2026-the-abstraction-gap-in-vision-.tldr: CAGE separates fluent causal explanations from explicit causal chains, revealing large gaps in seven of eight evaluated vision-language models.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts language models activate only a subset of their parameters for each token. This paper asks whether that sparsity also makes their internal computation easier to interpret. The authors compare neurons inside experts with neurons in dense feed-forward networks using k-sparse probing to assess how many meanings neurons appear to represent.

Expert neurons are consistently less polysemantic, meaning their activity mixes fewer distinct meanings. The difference grows as routing becomes sparser. This suggests that sparse activation encourages more specific roles at both the neuron and expert levels, motivating the authors to interpret entire experts as useful units of analysis.

The researchers automatically interpret hundreds of experts. Their analysis characterizes experts as specializing in fine-grained linguistic operations or semantic tasks, such as closing LaTeX brackets, rather than fitting broad domain or simple token-level descriptions. These findings suggest that expert-level interpretation can provide a clearer route to analyzing MoE models at scale. The evidence supports this interpretation of the studied experts without making sparsity a universal guarantee of transparent behavior.
icml-2026-the-expert-strikes-back-interp.tldr: MoE experts show less mixed neuron meanings and appear to specialize in fine-grained tasks, making experts useful units for interpretation.

paragraphs: This theoretical paper asks how combining regression predictors changes what can be learned and how much data learning requires. It studies the interaction between interpolation and aggregation, establishing that a complexity measure called the gamma-graph dimension characterizes learnability for a broad class of natural aggregation procedures.

Within that class, a remarkably simple rule is optimal: combine three interpolating hypotheses by taking their median prediction. The authors also show that this procedure is strictly more powerful than proper learning, where the learner must return a hypothesis from the original class. Combining predictions can therefore expand learning capability beyond choosing a single member of that class.

The paper also identifies a boundary to this result. Some hypothesis classes require aggregating infinitely many hypotheses or using non-interpolating aggregation rules that may predict outside the range of their inputs. For these classes, every finite interpolating aggregation fails to achieve even trivial performance. The findings jointly explain the strength of a small median-based ensemble and why its optimality within the studied family does not imply universal learnability.
icml-2026-the-interplay-between-interpol.tldr: The median of three interpolating predictors is optimal within a broad aggregation family, but some regression classes require more permissive rules.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn a linear contract from existing data when agent types follow an unknown distribution. The principal wants a contract that maximizes expected utility. The central question is how many samples are needed to choose a contract whose utility is close to the best available linear contract.

The authors prove that Empirical Utility Maximization achieves an epsilon approximation with probability at least 1 minus delta using O(ln(1/delta)/epsilon²) samples. This procedure selects according to utility measured on the observed data. The sample bound improves previous guarantees and matches an existing lower bound up to constant factors, establishing optimal sample complexity for the stated setting.

The analysis also provides uniform convergence at the same sample complexity: empirical utility approximates expected utility for every linear contract simultaneously, with the stated probability. This is stronger than guaranteeing only that the selected contract performs well. It explains why optimizing the empirical objective is reliable even though the contract is chosen after observing the data, rather than fixed in advance.
icml-2026-the-optimal-sample-complexity-.tldr: Empirical Utility Maximization learns near-optimal linear contracts with provably optimal sample complexity and a uniform utility-estimation guarantee.

paragraphs: Some high-frequency control systems need to adapt on sub-microsecond timescales. Meeting that requirement means learning with limited memory, low latency, and fixed-precision arithmetic directly on hardware. This paper investigates Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks, or KANs, as an architecture suited to those constraints, where conventional multilayer perceptrons can be inefficient and numerically unstable.

The authors identify two helpful properties. B-spline locality makes updates sparse, so learning can update a limited portion of the model and scale on-chip resources more favorably. KANs also show robustness to fixed-point quantization. Together, these properties connect the network’s mathematical structure to the memory and arithmetic requirements of fast hardware learning.

The researchers implement fixed-point online training on FPGAs and compare KANs with multilayer perceptrons across low-latency, resource-constrained tasks. KAN learners are substantially more efficient and expressive in those evaluations. The authors describe the result, to their knowledge, as the first demonstration of model-free online learning below one microsecond. The contribution is an implemented connection between local spline updates and extremely fast adaptation.
icml-2026-ultrafast-on-chip-online-learn.tldr: KANs exploit sparse spline updates and fixed-point robustness to demonstrate sub-microsecond online learning on FPGAs.

paragraphs: Neural-network explanations often focus on what is present: pixels that support a prediction or patterns that strongly activate a neuron. This paper examines another possibility, encoded absence, where a neuron activates more strongly because a concept is missing. Such evidence can be difficult to expose using standard explanation methods.

The authors show that these missing-but-relevant concepts are common and that mainstream attribution and feature-visualization techniques struggle to reveal them in their usual form. They propose two simple extensions to those techniques. The aim is to make absence visible within familiar explanation tools, expanding the kinds of relationships those tools can uncover.

Experiments demonstrate how the extended methods reveal encoded absences and how ImageNet models use them. The paper also finds that accounting for such absences can improve debiasing. This matters because explaining only visible supporting features can leave part of a model’s decision process unexamined. The results broaden the interpretation of neuron activity: a strong response can reflect missing information as well as a detected concept.
icml-2026-what-is-missing-explaining-neu.tldr: Simple extensions to explanation methods reveal neurons activated by missing concepts and can improve debiasing.

paragraphs: Model repositories often contain checkpoints with little documentation, creating a need to identify and analyze models from their parameters. Processing all weights directly is expensive. Probing methods provide a lighter alternative by extracting representations with learnable vectors, but existing single-view approaches miss higher-order relationships between weight-matrix rows and columns.

MVProbe combines first-order signals with interaction-aware views built from Gram-based representations. This gives the representation access to correlation patterns beyond those captured by the original probing view. The authors also analyze how different probing orders scale, deriving a standardization and fusion strategy intended to balance contributions from the different branches.

On the Model Jungle benchmark, MVProbe consistently outperforms ProbeX across ResNet, SupViT, MAE, and DINO architectures. These results support combining complementary views when representing a model through its weights. The theoretical scaling analysis matters because adding branches alone does not ensure balanced influence: the fusion strategy addresses how signals of different orders enter the combined representation. The contribution is richer lightweight probing with a principled way to combine its components.
icml-2026-what-linear-probes-miss-multi-.tldr: MVProbe combines first-order and correlation-aware weight probes, outperforming ProbeX across several architectures on Model Jungle.
